section.title: Why approximate integrals?
section.p: A definite integral is an exact idea. Numerical integration is the art of computing a usable approximation to that exact idea.
This is not a retreat from calculus. It is one of the main ways calculus is used.

note.title: Data form of the integral problem
note.p: A table can give enough information to estimate an integral, even when it does not give enough information to find an exact antiderivative.

subsection.p: This happens constantly: velocity from GPS samples, temperature from a probe, force from a sensor, power usage from a meter, rainfall from a weather station, and density from measurements along a rod.
The integral still means accumulation. Only the method of computation changes.

exercise.title: Why can a table still define an integral problem?

statement.p: A force sensor may give only a table of values, not a formula for F(x). In your own words, why is the work \int_a^b F(x)\,dx still a real quantity, and what information does the table give that an antiderivative formula would have given?

hint.p: The integral still means accumulation. A table supplies samples of the integrand, not an elementary antiderivative.

subsection.p: Sometimes we do have a formula, but the formula has no antiderivative built from the elementary functions of this course.

note.title: Important distinction
note.p: A function can be easy to evaluate but hard to antidifferentiate.
Numerical integration uses values of the function directly. It does not require an elementary antiderivative.

exercise.title: Why can a function be easy to evaluate but hard to antidifferentiate?

statement.p: The integrand e^{-x^2} is continuous and easy to compute, yet \int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx cannot be finished by the Fundamental Theorem with elementary functions. In your own words, what distinction does that example make, and why does numerical integration still make sense?

hint.p: Existence of a definite integral is about the integrand, not about whether an antiderivative is elementary. Numerical rules use values of f directly.

subsection.title: Speed versus accuracy
subsection.p: The original definition of the integral used Riemann sums:
If n is large and the function is well behaved, these sums can approximate the integral well. But a large n means many function evaluations.
There is a practical tradeoff:
The word “usually” matters. More samples help when they are used intelligently and when the function is well behaved on the interval. They do not automatically fix every problem.

For example, if the integrand has a sharp spike, a coarse grid may miss it. If the integral is improper, applying a rule directly at an infinite endpoint or a vertical asymptote may make no sense. If a computer subtracts nearly equal numbers many times, roundoff error may accumulate.

exercise.title: Why is more sampling not automatically better?

statement.p: Riemann sums suggest that a larger n should improve an approximation. In your own words, why is that only usually true, and what can go wrong even if you take many samples?

hint.p: Think about a missed spike, an improper integral, or arithmetic that subtracts nearly equal numbers. A rule without an error story is still a guess.

note.title: Numerical integration needs an error statement
note.p: A useful numerical answer should say something like

subsection.p: There are two common ways to judge an approximation.
First, if we know enough about the function, we can use an error bound. An error bound gives a guaranteed maximum possible error.

Second, if we compute several approximations using smaller and smaller step sizes, we can watch the values stabilize. This gives evidence, and often very good evidence, but it is not the same as a proof unless it is supported by a theorem.

exercise.title: What extra sentence makes a numerical answer useful?

statement.p: Suppose a computation reports \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx A. In your own words, why is that incomplete, and what is the difference between watching approximations stabilize and having an error bound?

hint.p: Absolute error is |I-A|. Stabilization is evidence. A bound is a guarantee, provided the hypotheses of the theorem hold.
